analysis.one_liner: Directs the government to negotiate lower Medicare prescription drug prices with manufacturers.
analysis.headline: A bill to let Medicare negotiate drug prices, introduced by one senator with no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have removed the 'noninterference' rule that bars the Health and Human Services Secretary from negotiating drug prices for Medicare's Part D benefit, and directed the Secretary to negotiate prices, discounts, and rebates with pharmaceutical manufacturers on behalf of Medicare beneficiaries. It preserved the ban on government-mandated formularies and required the Secretary to report negotiation results to Congress twice a year. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare's roughly tens of millions of Part D enrollees, who pay premiums and out-of-pocket drug costs tied to the prices plans pay, would gain if the government negotiated lower prices. Taxpayers also benefit, since Medicare subsidizes a large share of Part D drug costs, so lower prices reduce federal spending.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the statutory 'noninterference' provision and requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate with pharmaceutical manufacturers the prices, discounts, rebates, and other price concessions that may be charged to Part D plan sponsors for covered drugs [S2] [S3].
It takes effect immediately on enactment and first applies to plan years beginning January 1, 2011 [S3].
It requires semi-annual reports to Congress on the negotiations conducted and the price discounts achieved, creating public accountability for the results [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose Medicare Part D revenues would come under direct government price negotiation for the first time since the benefit was created in 2003. To the extent negotiations cut manufacturer revenue, industry groups argued this could reduce investment in developing new drugs.

drawbacks.text: Government price negotiation would cut deeply into brand-name drug makers' Medicare revenue, and the industry's standard good-faith objection is that lower expected prices mean less money for researching future drugs. Opponents also argued that private plans and their pharmacy benefit managers already negotiate discounts, so a government negotiator would add a layer rather than replace one (the bill does not bar plans from seeking deeper discounts below the negotiated price) [S3].

The bill directs negotiation but leaves the mechanics open — which drugs, what targets, what leverage — so its real-world savings would have depended entirely on how the Secretary implemented it, and critics could fairly question whether a mandate without strong enforcement tools would achieve much [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets one of the clearest mismatches in American health care: the largest single drug buyer in the country is legally barred from using its bargaining power. The main honest cost is to brand-name manufacturers' revenue, with a secondary risk, not proven either way in this record, that lower prices could modestly slow future drug development. The design is narrow and careful — no formulary mandates, plans free to negotiate deeper discounts — which limits both its upside and its downside.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day, and the committee never took it up; it died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Sen. Feingold introduced the bill on May 25, 2010; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
The Finance Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers came out ahead: the statutory ban on Medicare price negotiation, which this bill would have repealed, stayed in place, and manufacturers kept charging Medicare plans list-based prices with no government negotiator across the table.

for.name: Sen. Russell Feingold
for.role: U.S. Senator from Wisconsin and sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Finance Committee; no other senator joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Chair Max Baucus and the Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Fought government price negotiation for Medicare drugs for years, including during the 2009-2010 health reform debate, to keep the noninterference clause in place.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.role: Minority caucus opposing Medicare price negotiation
against.what_they_did: Consistently opposed giving the government negotiating authority over Part D drug prices, which Republicans helped write into the 2003 Medicare law creating Part D.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows no vote and no cosponsors, so no partisan split is measurable here: a bill on an issue that usually divides the parties attracted support from only one of the Senate's 59 Democrats or independents.

industries.note: The bill would have ended the statutory ban on Medicare price negotiation and let the government bargain directly over Part D drug prices, directly cutting into manufacturers' largest public-program revenue stream. Because manufacturers profit from charging Medicare plans higher prices, their interest runs against beneficiaries' pocketbooks here.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D plans and Medicare Advantage insurers
industries.note: Negotiated prices would lower what plans pay for drugs, squeezing margins on the benefit they administer, but lower prices also reduce plan premium pressure. The bill leaves plans free to seek deeper discounts than the government negotiates.
A government negotiator competing at the top of the market would have eroded the leverage PBMs sell to plans, though the bill preserves plans' ability to use PBM discounts below the negotiated price.
